t: What an Under-Desk Cable Management Tray Is
title: What an Under-Desk Cable Management Tray Is
description: An under-desk cable management tray is a wire-mesh or metal basket that screws under the desk, holding power strips, adapters, and cable slack off the floor. Instead of a dusty tangle underfoot, everything lives in a ventilated basket: power comes up from the wall into the tray, cables drop from the desk into the tray, and one clean trunk exits. The IKEA SIGNUM is the classic; wire baskets are the workhorses.

demo.program:
print("Tray: ventilated basket under desk. Power in from wall, cables down from desk,")
print("one clean trunk out. Floor tangle -> organized basket.")
print("IKEA SIGNUM: the classic. Wire mesh: the workhorse.")

title: How Trays Change the Under-Desk: Before and After

t: Tray Types: Wire Mesh, Solid Metal, and Fabric
title: Tray Types: Wire Mesh, Solid Metal, and Fabric
description: Wire mesh trays: ventilated (heat escapes), see-through (find cables fast), the practical default. Solid metal: sturdier, cleaner look, heavier, pricier. Fabric/nylon: cheap, soft, sags under bricks — fine for light cable-only duty, wrong for power strips. For bricks and strips, wire mesh or solid metal; for cables only, fabric is acceptable.

demo.program:
print("wire mesh: ventilated, see-through. PRACTICAL DEFAULT (bricks + strips).")
print("solid metal: sturdy, clean, heavy, pricier.")
print("fabric: cheap, sags under bricks. Cables-only duty at most.")

t: Sizing: Matching Tray to Desk and Gear
title: Sizing: Matching Tray to Desk and Gear
description: Size the tray to the gear, not the desk: measure the power strip plus the two biggest bricks side by side, add 4 inches for cable slack and fingers. Common trays run 15-40 inches wide; a 24-inch tray swallows a strip plus two bricks comfortably. Depth 4-6 inches clears most bricks; shallow trays choke on big adapters. Measure the gear first — the #1 sizing mistake is buying for the desk, not the load.

demo.program:
strip_in, brick_in = 12, 8
need = strip_in + brick_in + 4
print(f"Strip {strip_in} in + brick {brick_in} in + 4 in slack = {need} in tray width.")
print("Depth 4-6 in clears most bricks. Shallow trays choke on big adapters.")
print("Measure GEAR first: #1 mistake is sizing for the desk, not the load.")

title: Installation: Mounting Under the Desk
description: Mount with the included screws into the desk's underside — solid wood takes screws directly; particle board wants pilot holes to avoid splitting; glass or thin tops need clamp-mount trays instead of screws. Position: back third of the desk, reachable but out of knee space. Two-person job for wide trays: one holds, one drives. Verify no knee collision before loading.

print("Glass/thin: clamp-mount trays (no screws).")
print("Position: back third, out of knee space. Wide trays: 2-person mount.")
print("Knee-check BEFORE loading.")

t: What Lives in the Tray: The Load Plan
title: What Lives in the Tray: The Load Plan
description: The tray holds: the power strip (the hub), brick adapters (laptop, monitor), cable slack (coiled, velcro-strapped), and the trunk's top end. It does NOT hold: anything hot without ventilation (mesh helps, but check), heavy UPS units (floor those), or the rat's nest 'temporarily'. Every item in the tray has a reason; the tray is infrastructure, not a junk drawer.

t: Power Strip Orientation and Safety in Trays
title: Power Strip Orientation and Safety in Trays
description: Mount the strip with outlets facing up or sideways for easy plugging, never facing down where plugs strain. Keep the strip's switch accessible — you will need it. Do not daisy-chain strips in the tray (one strip per wall outlet), respect the strip's amperage rating, and keep the tray ventilated around bricks. A tidy tray is also a safer tray: no strain, no chains, no buried switches.

print("Outlets up/sideways (never down: plug strain). Switch ACCESSIBLE.")
print("One strip per wall outlet (no daisy chains). Respect amperage rating.")
print("Ventilate bricks. Tidy = safe: no strain, no chains, no buried switches.")

t: Routing Into the Tray: From Desk and Wall
title: Routing Into the Tray: From Desk and Wall
description: Cables drop from the desk edge (via clips) into the tray's back; power comes from the wall outlet up into the tray's side. Keep the wall-to-tray run short and anchored — it is the one cable that never moves. Label both ends of every tray cable (the tray hides them, labels find them). The tray is the junction: desk above, wall beside, floor trunk below.

t: Use Case: Standing Desks and Moving Trays
title: Use Case: Standing Desks and Moving Trays
description: Standing desks move — the tray must move with it, with cable slack for the full height range. Mount the tray to the moving desktop (not the fixed frame), leave a service loop in every cable for max height, and anchor the wall power with enough slack to reach the top position. Test full up/down travel before calling it done; a cable that goes taut at max height will fail.

demo.program:
print("Tray mounts to MOVING desktop (not fixed frame).")
print("Service loop per cable for full height range.")
print("Test FULL up/down travel: taut at max height = future failure.")

title: Ventilation and Heat in Trays
description: Bricks generate heat; trays must breathe. Wire mesh is naturally ventilated — the reason it is the default. Do not pack bricks tight against each other; leave finger-width gaps. In warm rooms, check brick temps seasonally — a brick too hot to hold needs spacing or a fan. Heat trapped in a tray shortens adapter life silently.

demo.program:
print("Mesh = ventilated (the default for a reason).")
print("Finger-width gaps between bricks. Hot-to-hold = needs spacing/air.")
print("Trapped heat shortens adapter life SILENTLY. Check seasonally.")

title: Trays vs Raceways vs J-Channels
description: Trays: hold bricks, strips, and slack — the heavy-duty under-desk answer. Raceways: covered strips hiding cable runs along surfaces — cleaner look, no brick capacity. J-channels: open hooks guiding cables — cheapest, least hidden. The under-desk usually wants a tray (for the bricks) plus a raceway or J-channel (for the runs): hold plus hide.

print("raceway  : covered strip, hides runs, no brick capacity.")
print("J-channel: open hooks, cheapest, least hidden.")
print("Under-desk: tray (hold) + raceway/J (hide the runs).")

title: Maintenance: The Semiannual Tray Audit
description: Twice a year, empty the tray: dust it out, check every brick's temp rating vs its load, replace any warm cables, re-coil slack neatly, verify labels, and remove anything that migrated in 'temporarily'. The audit takes twenty minutes and prevents the tray's slow slide into a junk basket. The tray stays infrastructure because someone checks.

title: Buying Guide: What to Check
description: Check: width vs your gear measurement, depth vs your biggest brick, mounting hardware for your desk material (or clamp version), weight rating (bricks are heavy — 10+ lbs capacity), and ventilation (mesh preferred). Expect 20-45 dollars. The 12-dollar fabric sacks sag under a real strip — buy the tray once.

print("      weight rating 10+ lbs | mesh ventilation.")
print("$20-45. $12 fabric sags under real strips: buy the tray ONCE.")
